lesson.title: Separable Verb Gym
lesson.subtitle: opbellen, meebrengen, aankomen, uitwaaien, overstappen, pinnen

hook.title: Split the Verb, Park the Prefix
hook.content: Six verbs, one habit: find the prefix, keep the finite part second, send the prefix to the end. Some verbs look separable and are not — pinnen stays whole.

pattern.title: Prefix at the end, finite part second
pattern.content: Ik bel mijn moeder op, ik breng een boek mee, de trein komt aan, wij stappen over. The prefix can be a direction, a completion or a separation.
pattern.trap_note: Not every prefix-like syllable separates. Pinnen has no separable prefix; it stays a single verb.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Separable Verb Gym):

matching_pairs.english: to clear one's head in the wind

exercises.target_answer: opbellen, meebrengen, aankomen, uitwaaien, overstappen, pinnen
exercises.meaning: to call (phone), to bring along, to arrive, to clear one's head in the wind, to change trains, to pay by card
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Separable Verb Gym": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “I call my mother.”?
options: niet Ik bel mijn moeder op.
exercises.explanation: “Ik bel mijn moeder op.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Separable Verb Gym”.

cues: The pattern: Prefix at the end, finite part second
It means: I bring a book along.
exercises.explanation: “Ik breng een boek mee.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Prefix at the end, finite part second.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Not every prefix-like syllable separates. Pinnen has no separable prefix; it stays a single verb.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “De trein komt aan.” is word-for-word “The train comes at.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Prefix at the end, finite part second.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: I pay by card here.
exercises.explanation: “Ik pin hier.” reuses only material taught in “Separable Verb Gym” — Prefix at the end, finite part second.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Ik pin hier.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Prefix at the end, finite part second.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “We change trains.”
twist.explanation: Overstappen splits: stappen is finite, over closes the sentence.

summary.outcome: Split five separable verbs correctly and leave a non-separable verb whole.
summary.takeaway: The prefix is a position, not a decoration; the sentence tells you where it goes.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Numbers & Time.

opbellen.etymology_derivation: Separable: op + bellen. A bell was the old way to call someone.

uitwaaien.english_meaning: to clear one's head in the wind
uitwaaien.context_translation: I am going to clear my head in the wind.

pinnen.etymology_derivation: From the PIN of a bank card; Dutch turned the acronym into a verb.
